questions.q: An agricultural extension officer working with farmers in the Eritrean highlands and western lowlands is preparing a planting plan based on the agronomic classification of field crops given in the unit. The crops under consideration are: teff, niger seed (nihug), faba bean, cotton, sorghum, sesame and sugarcane. (a) Sort all seven crops into their correct agronomic groups (cereals, pulses, industrial crops, forage crops). (b) Name the sub-groups of the industrial crops into which niger seed, cotton and sugarcane fall. (c) The officer advises a farmer who grew sorghum this season to rotate it next season with faba bean rather than with another cereal. Using the unit's description of pulses, justify this advice with one biological reason. (d) Which of the seven crops is a native of the Abyssinian center of diversity, and what does teff's origin there tell us about the crop?
questions.answer: (a) Cereals: teff and sorghum. Pulses: faba bean. Industrial crops: niger seed (oil), sesame (oil), cotton (fiber) and sugarcane (sugar). Forage crops: none of the seven crops listed. (b) Niger seed and sesame = oil crops; cotton = fiber crop; sugarcane = sugar crop. (c) Pulses such as faba bean are leguminous plants able to fix atmospheric nitrogen in the soil, so a faba bean crop restores the nitrogen that the sorghum cereal removed, improving soil fertility for the next crop. (d) Teff is native to the Abyssinian center of diversity (Eritrean Highlands); because its wild progenitor Eragrostis pilosa is native there, teff was domesticated locally thousands of years ago.
why: **Recall the four agronomic groups.** The unit classifies field crops as cereals (grown for edible starchy seeds, rich in carbohydrates), pulses (leguminous plants grown for protein-rich seeds and valued for fixing atmospheric nitrogen), industrial crops (raw materials for industries), and forage crops (grown as livestock feed, preserved as hay or silage or grazed).
**Assign the cereals.** Teff (Eragrostis tef) and sorghum are stated in the unit to be cereals because they are grown for their edible starchy seeds; the unit's cereal examples include both.
**Assign the pulse.** Faba bean (Vicia faba) is listed in the unit's crop table as a pulse (legume), so it forms the single pulse entry among the seven crops.

**Assign the industrial crops and their sub-groups.** Niger seed (nihug) and sesame are oil crops, cotton is a fiber crop and sugarcane is a sugar crop, so all four are industrial crops. The unit's sub-groups are oil crops (sesame, linseed), sugar crops (sugarcane, sugar beet) and fiber crops (cotton, sisal).

**Check for forage crops.** None of the seven crops is described in the unit as a forage crop: forage crops are grown specifically as livestock feed and conserved as hay or silage. The forage group therefore has no member in this list, which is an important negative finding for the officer's plan.

**Justify the rotation advice (part c).** The unit states that pulses are leguminous plants valued for their ability to fix atmospheric nitrogen in the soil. Sorghum, as a cereal, takes nutrients out of the soil during the season, whereas a faba bean crop adds nitrogen to the soil. Rotating sorghum with faba bean therefore restores soil nitrogen and improves the fertility of the field for the following cereal crop.

**Identify the Abyssinian native and interpret it (part d).** The unit's table gives teff's native center of diversity as the Abyssinian Center (Eritrean Highlands); niger seed, barley, emmer wheat, linseed, safflower, chickpea, lentil and sesame are also named as crops domesticated there. The unit's Did You Know note adds that the wild progenitor of cultivated teff, Eragrostis pilosa, is native to this center, which confirms that teff was domesticated locally thousands of years ago.

**Conclude the classification.** Cereals: teff, sorghum. Pulse: faba bean. Industrial crops (oil): niger seed, sesame; (fiber): cotton; (sugar): sugarcane. Forage: none of the seven. Rotation with faba bean is justified because pulses fix atmospheric nitrogen, and teff belongs to the Abyssinian center of diversity, confirming local domestication.

questions.q: A farmer in the Eritrean highlands plans a four-field rotation and can choose from barley, linseed, chickpea and sisal. (b) Which two of these crops would you recommend the farmer grow in order to add nitrogen to the soil, and why? (b) Chickpea would be recommended, because it is a leguminous pulse valued for fixing atmospheric nitrogen in the soil; linseed is an oil crop and does not add nitrogen. (c) Sisal is grown as a raw material for industry (its fiber), whereas cereals are grown for their edible starchy seeds, so the two crops belong to different agronomic groups.
why: **Recall the classification criteria.** Cereals are grown for edible starchy seeds rich in carbohydrates; pulses are legumes grown for protein-rich seeds and for nitrogen fixation; industrial crops are raw materials for industries, including oil crops (sesame, linseed) and fiber crops (cotton, sisal).
**Classify each of the four crops.** Barley is named in the unit as a cereal; linseed appears in the unit's oil crop examples; chickpea is named among pulses; sisal is listed as a fiber crop.

**Answer part (b).** Only chickpea is a leguminous pulse able to fix atmospheric nitrogen, so it is the crop that adds nitrogen to the soil; linseed, barley and sisal do not have this property in the unit.

**Answer part (c).** Sisal is a fiber crop because it is grown as an industrial raw material, while a cereal is grown for its edible starchy seed; the harvested product and the purpose of growing it are therefore completely different.

questions.q: Three Eritrean buyers place orders with a farming cooperative: an oil press needs raw material, a flour mill needs starchy grain, and a textile factory needs natural fiber. From the crops teff, niger seed, sesame, chickpea, cotton and sugarcane, (a) select one crop for each buyer and name the agronomic group it belongs to; (b) state which of the six crops are pulses and explain the soil benefit they provide; (c) name the industrial sub-group of any remaining crop that is an industrial crop but was not chosen in (a).
questions.answer: (a) Oil press: niger seed or sesame (oil crops within the industrial crops group). Flour mill: teff (cereal). Textile factory: cotton (fiber crop within the industrial crops group). (b) Chickpea is the only pulse among the six; as a leguminous plant it fixes atmospheric nitrogen in the soil and so improves soil fertility. (c) The remaining industrial crop is sugarcane, which is a sugar crop.
why: **Match each buyer to a crop group.** The unit's industrial crops include oil crops (sesame, linseed), fiber crops (cotton, sisal) and sugar crops (sugarcane, sugar beet); cereals are grown for edible starchy seeds. An oil press needs an oil crop, a flour mill needs a cereal, and a textile factory needs a fiber crop.
**Answer part (a).** Oil press: niger seed or sesame. Flour mill: teff, because teff is a cereal with starchy grain. Textile factory: cotton, because cotton is a fiber crop.

**Answer part (b).** Chickpea is the only pulse listed; the unit states that pulses are leguminous plants grown for protein-rich seeds and valued for their ability to fix atmospheric nitrogen in the soil, which raises soil fertility for the next crop.
**Answer part (c).** Sugarcane was not selected by any of the three buyers and is an industrial crop of the sugar crop sub-group.
**Check that no crop is left unclassified.** Teff = cereal; niger seed and sesame = oil crops; cotton = fiber crop; sugarcane = sugar crop; chickpea = pulse. All six crops are accounted for.

similar.a: Olericulture.

similar.q: Floriculture deals with?

similar.q: In which system are temperature, light and humidity controlled?
similar.a: A greenhouse (glasshouse).

questions.label: 3.5 Practice — horticulture

questions.q: A nursery that keeps seedlings from a standard nursery for a short time before distribution is
why: Step 1: Peasant = farmer’s own; standard = commercial; intermediate = short-term holding.

similar.q: What is a peasant nursery?
similar.a: Where rural farmers raise their own seedlings.

questions.label: 3.5 Practice — horticulture

questions.q: List five criteria for selecting a nursery site.
questions.answer: Suitable climate and shelter from wind; level land; clean water free of salts; fertile soil; easy road access (and a fence against animals).
why: Step 1: Weather and wind.
Step 2: Land and soil.
Step 3: Water and access.

similar.q: What is the first step in preparing a nursery site?
similar.a: Site clearing, then levelling and layout.

questions.label: 3.5 Practice — horticulture

questions.q: In dry areas with little rain, nursery seedlings are best raised in
why: Step 1: Sunken beds (10–15 cm below ground) hold water.
Step 2: Raised beds (15–20 cm up) drain water in wet areas.

similar.q: How high is a raised bed?
similar.a: 15–20 cm above ground.

questions.label: 3.5 Practice — horticulture

questions.q: Describe the damage weeds cause in a nursery and the cheapest way to control them.
questions.answer: They compete strongly for nutrients and water in small containers (and for light if left uncontrolled), and harbour pests; good sanitation is the cheapest control, with hand weeding of young weeds.
why: Step 1: Small soil volume → severe competition.
Step 2: Prevention by sanitation.

similar.q: Why is grading done in a nursery?
similar.a: To discard poor seedlings that would die or yield poorly; 10–20 % culls is normal.

questions.label: 3.5 Practice — horticulture

questions.q: In a grafted orange tree, the part that carries the desired fruit variety is the
why: Step 1: Scion = upper part, the variety.
Step 2: Rootstock = lower root system.

similar.q: Which tissue must be matched for a graft to take?
similar.a: The cambium.

questions.label: 3.5 Practice — horticulture

questions.q: Give the main steps of T-budding.
questions.answer: Make a vertical cut 3–4 cm and a horizontal cut 1–2 cm through the stock bark (a T); cut a bud shield with a thin sliver of wood; open the flaps and push in the shield; wrap with tape leaving the bud exposed.
why: Step 1: T-cut.
Step 2: Shield.
Step 3: Insert.
Step 4: Wrap.

similar.q: Which fruit is most commonly budded?
similar.a: Citrus.

questions.label: 3.5 Practice — horticulture

questions.q: Whip grafting is suitable for stems about
why: Step 1: Whip grafts join small stems of equal size, 6–12 mm.
Step 2: Large stems use bark or cleft grafts.

similar.q: Which grafts are used to top-work large trees?
similar.a: Bark and cleft grafting.

questions.label: 3.5 Practice — horticulture

questions.q: Distinguish softwood and hardwood cuttings.
questions.answer: Softwood: young soft shoots 10–15 cm, leaves removed from the lower third, kept under mist. Hardwood: dormant wood 6–20 mm thick, 15–30 cm long, callused in moist peat (upside down) before planting.
why: Step 1: Age and softness of wood.
Step 2: Length and treatment.
questions.tip: Soft needs mist; hard needs callus.

similar.q: Name three plants easily raised from cuttings.
similar.a: Lantana, grape and coleus.

questions.q: Removing a ring of bark from a branch and wrapping it in moist moss and plastic is
why: Step 1: The branch roots in the air, still on the tree.
questions.tip: Air layering = rooting in the air.

similar.q: Which layering pegs a branch down at several points?
similar.a: Serpentine (compound) layering.

questions.label: 3.5 Practice — horticulture

questions.q: Banana and date palm are usually propagated by
why: Step 1: They form suckers/offshoots at the base.
Step 2: These are separated and planted.

similar.q: Name two plants propagated by bulbs.
similar.a: Garlic and onion (also narcissus).

questions.label: 3.5 Practice — horticulture

questions.q: Give three hardening practices for nursery seedlings.
questions.answer: Expose them to below-optimum temperatures (cool areas) or above-optimum (hot areas); reduce water gradually without wilting; move shaded seedlings gradually into full sun.
why: Step 1: Temperature.
Step 2: Water.
Step 3: Light.
questions.tip: Toughen with temperature, water and sun.

similar.q: Why harden seedlings?
similar.a: So they survive transplant shock, root faster and resist drought.

questions.label: 3.5 Practice — horticulture

questions.q: Indicate the major factors in choosing a site for a horticultural farm.
questions.answer: Climate (temperature, rain, light, wind); terrain (altitude, slope); soil and drainage; availability of irrigation water; economics (profit, market).
why: Step 1: Physical factors.
Step 2: Water.
Step 3: Money.

similar.q: Why is site selection more critical for an orchard than for vegetables?
similar.a: Fruit trees are perennial and cannot easily be moved.

questions.label: 3.5 Practice — horticulture

questions.q: In double digging, how deep is the bed loosened and how often is it repeated?
questions.answer: 45–60 cm deep; every 2–4 years (in medium and clay soils).
why: Step 1: Topsoil 28–30 cm + subsoil 15–30 cm.
Step 2: Repeat after 2–4 years.

similar.q: What pit size is used for most fruit trees?
similar.a: 60 × 60 × 60 cm (100 cm in hardpan soil).

questions.label: 3.5 Practice — horticulture

questions.q: When is a tomato seedling ready to transplant?
questions.answer: At 4–6 true leaves, 15–20 cm tall with a pencil-thick stocky stem, after about 3–6 weeks in warm climates.
why: Step 1: Count true leaves.
Step 2: Check height and stem thickness.

similar.q: Why are old seedlings not recommended?
similar.a: Greater transplant shock; roots are damaged more.

questions.label: 3.5 Practice — horticulture

questions.q: Give three benefits of mulching.
questions.answer: Reduces evaporation and runoff; keeps soil temperature and moisture even; suppresses weeds (organic mulch also adds organic matter).
why: Step 1: Water saving.
Step 2: Temperature.
Step 3: Weeds.

similar.q: Give one organic and one inorganic mulch.
similar.a: Straw (or banana leaves) and plastic sheet.

questions.label: 3.5 Practice — horticulture

questions.q: A farmer harvests 300 kg of tomatoes and loses 30 % on the way to market. How many kilograms reach the market?
why: Step 1: Loss = 0.30 × 300 = 90 kg.
Step 2: Left = 300 − 90 = 210 kg.

similar.q: With only 10 % loss?

questions.label: 3.5 Practice — horticulture

questions.q: How does post-harvest handling affect the quality and quantity of horticultural products?
questions.answer: Bad handling (bruising, heat, delay, wrong packing) causes losses up to 50 % and poor quality; good handling (harvest in cool hours, clean, sort, grade, pack in crates, quick shaded transport) keeps produce fresh and saleable.
why: Step 1: Produce is alive and perishable.
Step 2: Each step either protects or damages it.

similar.q: Which needs boxes rather than sacks: potato or tomato?
similar.a: Tomato.
